Section 1.3 of Lock⁵ asks the central question of data collection: **when does an
association justify a causal conclusion?** In an **observational study** researchers
merely record the explanatory and response variables as they occur, so a third,
**confounding variable** — one that is associated with the explanatory variable and
is itself a cause of the response — may account for the association. In a
**randomized experiment** the researchers actively impose the explanatory variable
and assign it at random, which balances confounders between the groups and licenses
causal conclusions. Well-designed experiments use **control groups** for comparison,
**placebos** to counter the placebo effect, **blinding** (single- or double-blind)
to hide who gets which treatment, and enough **replication**; the two standard
designs are the **randomized comparative experiment** (separate groups) and the
**matched pairs** experiment (each case measured under both conditions).
The exercises below are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data*
(Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 45–51). Skill Builders 1.76–1.91 classify headline claims,
hunt for confounders, and tell experiments from observational studies; 1.92–1.94
revisit questions first asked in Section 1.1; 1.95–1.124 apply the ideas to real
studies, including several where you design the experiment yourself. Tabs based on
Lock5 data files include a small executable EDA.

## Exercise 1.76

**“Daily exercise improves mental performance.”**
*(Skill Builder 1: state whether the claim is one of association and causation, association only, or neither.)*

- **Association and causation.** “Improves” claims both that mental performance
  differs between people who exercise daily and those who do not (association) and
  that the exercise is what produces the better performance (causation).

## Exercise 1.77

**“Among college students, no link found between number of friends on social
networking websites and size of the university.”**

- **Neither association nor causation.** The headline explicitly reports finding
  *no link*, so no association is claimed — and without an association there is
  certainly no claim of causation.

## Exercise 1.78

**“Cell phone radiation leads to deaths in honey bees.”**

- **Association and causation.** “Leads to” asserts that the radiation causes the
  deaths (and, implicitly, that the two are associated).

## Exercise 1.79

**“Wealthy people are more likely than other folks to lie, cheat, and steal.”**

- **Association only.** “More likely than” compares groups — an association between
  wealth and dishonest behavior — but the headline does not claim that wealth
  *causes* anyone to behave badly.

## Exercise 1.80

**“Cat owners tend to be more educated than dog owners.”**

- **Association only.** A comparison of education levels between two groups of pet
  owners, with no causal language anywhere in the headline.

## Exercise 1.81

**“Want to lose weight? Eat more fiber!”**

- **Association and causation.** The advice implies that eating more fiber will
  *cause* weight loss, not merely that fiber intake and weight happen to be
  associated.

## Exercise 1.82

**More ice cream sales have been linked to more deaths by drowning.**
*(Skill Builder 2: give a confounding variable that may help account for the association.)*

- **Confounder: hot weather (season/temperature).** In hot weather people buy more
  ice cream *and* more people go swimming, so drownings increase. Weather is
  associated with the explanatory variable (ice cream sales) and is itself a cause
  of the response (drownings) — exactly the definition of a confounding variable.

## Exercise 1.83

**The total amount of beef consumed and the total amount of pork consumed worldwide
are closely related over the past 100 years.**

- **Confounder: world population.** As the human population has grown over the past
  century, total consumption of *both* meats has risen with it. Population is
  positively associated with each variable and plausibly causes part of both.
  (Growth of the world economy would serve equally well.)

## Exercise 1.84

**People who own a yacht are more likely to buy a sports car.**

- **Confounder: wealth.** Wealthier people are more likely to own a yacht and also
  more likely to buy a sports car. Wealth is associated with each variable and
  helps cause both purchases.

## Exercise 1.85

**Sales of toboggans tend to be higher when sales of mittens are higher.**

- **Confounder: winter weather (cold, snowy conditions).** Cold and snow send
  people out to buy both toboggans and mittens, producing the association between
  the two sets of sales.

## Exercise 1.86

**Air pollution is higher in places with a higher proportion of paved ground
relative to grassy ground.**

- **Confounder: size of the city (degree of urbanization).** Larger, more urban
  places have both more pavement relative to grass and more traffic and industry,
  hence more air pollution.

## Exercise 1.87

**People with shorter hair tend to be taller.**

- **Confounder: sex.** Men tend to be taller than women and, on average, wear their
  hair shorter. Sex is associated with hair length and directly influences height.

## Exercise 1.88

**To examine whether eating brown rice affects metabolism, ask a random sample of
people whether they eat brown rice and also measure their metabolism rate.**
*(Skill Builder 3: experiment or observational study?)*

- **Observational study.** The researchers only record an existing habit and measure
  a variable; nothing is imposed on the cases.

## Exercise 1.89

**To examine whether playing music in a store increases the amount customers spend,
randomly assign some stores to play music and some to stay silent and compare
average spending.**

- **Experiment.** The explanatory variable (music vs silence) is actively imposed by
  the researchers — and randomly assigned, at that.

## Exercise 1.90

**To examine whether planting trees reduces air pollution, plant trees in half of a
sample of similar city blocks and later measure pollution levels.**

- **Experiment.** The researchers control which blocks receive the treatment
  (trees), actively imposing the explanatory variable.

## Exercise 1.91

**To examine whether farm-grown salmon contain more omega-3 oils if water is more
acidic, collect salmon and water samples from multiple fish farms and see if the
variables are related.**

- **Observational study.** Existing farms are sampled as they are; the acidity of
  the water is not manipulated.

## Exercise 1.92

**“Is there a sprinting gene?”** *(Revisiting Section 1.1: introduced in Example 1.5
on page 9 — the *ACTN3* variant tested among world-class sprinters, world-class
marathon runners, and non-athletes.)*

- **Observational study.** The subjects arrived at their groups (and their genes) on
  their own; the researchers only recorded which group each person belongs to and
  whether they have the gene variant. No treatment was assigned to anyone.

## Exercise 1.93

**“Do metal tags on penguins harm them?”** *(Revisiting Section 1.1: Data 1.3 on
page 10 — 100 penguins followed for 10 years.)*

- **Experiment.** The penguins were *randomly given* either metal or electronic
  tags, so tag type — the explanatory variable — was assigned by the researchers.
  Later differences in survival, number of chicks, or foraging time can therefore
  support causal conclusions.

## Exercise 1.94

**“Are there human pheromones?”** *(Revisiting Section 1.1: three studies on
page 11 in which men were exposed to the scent of women’s tears or to a salt
solution. Indicate for each study whether it is an experiment or an observational
study.)*

- **Study 1 (pad on the upper lip, 25 men):** **Experiment** — researchers applied
  the “treatment” (tears vs salt solution) and measured how sexually alluring the
  men rated female faces.
- **Study 2 (sniffing, 50 men):** **Experiment** — the men were given tears or a
  salt solution to sniff and testosterone levels were compared.
- **Study 3 (sniffing, 16 men):** **Experiment** — again the substance sniffed was
  determined by the researchers, with brain-cell activity as the response.
- In all three studies the explanatory variable (tears vs salt solution) was
  actively administered rather than merely observed, which is what makes each an
  experiment.

## Exercise 1.95

**Salt on Roads and Accidents.** An association is described between the amount of
salt spread on roads and the number of accidents. Describe a possible confounding
variable and explain how it fits the definition.

- **Confounder: severity of the winter weather (or volume of traffic).** Towns that
  spread more salt are typically those with harsher, icier winters and busier roads
  — and those same conditions themselves cause more accidents. Weather is
  associated with salt use and is a direct cause of accidents, so it satisfies the
  definition of a confounding variable.

## Exercise 1.96

**Height and Reading Ability.** In elementary school (grades 1 to 6) taller children
tend to read at a higher level. A very significant confounding variable influences
both height and reading ability. What is it?

- **Confounder: age.** Within elementary school, older children are both taller and
  better readers. Age is associated with height and directly influences reading
  ability, so it accounts for much of the association between the two.

## Exercise 1.97

**Golfing for a Long Life?** A quote on a health site tells us “golfers’ average
life expectancy was 5 years longer than other people’s.”

- **(a) Cases:** the people whose life expectancy was reported (golfers and others).
  **Variables:** whether the person plays golf (**categorical**) and life expectancy
  (**quantitative**).
- **(b)** **Observational study** — nobody was assigned to become a golfer; people
  choose their own pastimes.
- **(c) Confounder: wealth.** Wealthier people can afford to golf and also enjoy
  better healthcare, nutrition, and working conditions. Wealth is associated with
  golfing and itself influences life expectancy, fitting the definition of a
  confounding variable. (General fitness/activity level would be another candidate.)

## Exercise 1.98

**How to Debate a Science Denier.** 1773 participants first listened to a science
denier and were then randomly assigned to one of four conditions: no rebuttal,
topic rebuttal, technique rebuttal, or both. Attitudes toward the science topic
were measured three times: before participation, after the science denier, and
after the rebuttal.

- **(a) Cases:** the 1773 participants.
- **(b) Explanatory variable:** the type of rebuttal received (none / topic /
  technique / both) — **categorical**. (The three time points organize the repeated
  attitude measurements, which serve as responses.)
- **(c)** **Experiment** — the rebuttal condition was randomly assigned.
- **(d)** **1773 rows** (one per participant). At minimum **4 columns**: the rebuttal
  condition plus the three attitude measurements (before, after the denier, after
  the rebuttal); any additional recorded variables would add more columns.

## Exercise 1.99

**Music Volume and Beer Consumption.** Researchers went into bars, controlled the
music volume according to a randomization scheme, and measured beer consumption.
Louder music corresponded to more beer consumed. Does this provide evidence that
louder music causes people to drink more beer? Why or why not?

- **Yes.** The volume was actively manipulated *and* randomly assigned, so
  confounding variables (type of bar, clientele, time of day, ...) are balanced
  between the loud and quiet settings. That is precisely the situation in which a
  causal conclusion is warranted — for the bars and settings studied.

## Exercise 1.100

**Nuts and Cholesterol.** In Study 1, participants were assigned to eat nuts each
day or to follow a nut-free diet. In Study 2, participants ate their own diets and
reported how many nuts they consumed. Both studies found nut consumption
associated with lower LDL cholesterol. Which study provides better evidence that
nut consumption reduces LDL cholesterol?

- **Study 1.** It is a randomized experiment: the researcher assigns the
  explanatory variable, so confounding variables (overall diet, health
  consciousness, income, ...) are balanced between the groups. In Study 2 people
  choose whether to eat nuts, so nut-eaters may differ systematically in other
  ways — a classic setup for confounding.

## Exercise 1.101

**Antibiotics in Infancy and Obesity in Adults.** In a mouse study, infant mice
were *randomly assigned* to receive antibiotics or not, and the treated mice were
more likely to be obese as adults. A separate human study found that children given
antibiotics before age one were more likely to be obese as adults. Is the headline
“Antibiotics in infancy may cause obesity in adults” appropriate:

- **(a) For mice? Yes.** The mouse study randomly assigned the antibiotics, so the
  association can reasonably be read as causal *for mice*.
- **(b) For humans? No.** The human study is observational: families differ in many
  ways associated with both antibiotic use and later obesity, so confounding is not
  ruled out. The causal headline is not appropriate for humans.

## Exercise 1.102

**Fast-Food Diet and Depression.** In a study of 84 middle-school students,
researchers measured urinary sodium and potassium (a marker of processed-food
intake) and evaluated depressive symptoms on a 100-point scale. High sodium and low
potassium were both associated with higher depression levels.

- **(a)** **Observational study.** Diets were not assigned; sodium and potassium
  were measured as they occurred.
- **(b) No.** We cannot conclude that the diet pattern *increases* the likelihood of
  depression: there is no random assignment, so only an association — not a causal
  link — has been established.
- **(c) Possible confounder: stress (or family income).** Students under more
  stress may both eat more convenient processed food and experience more depressive
  symptoms. Stress is associated with the explanatory variables and plausibly
  causes differences in the response, which fits the definition of a confounding
  variable.

## Exercise 1.103

**Potassium Levels in Spinach.** Spinach leaves from a variety of locations were
examined; spinach grown in soil with high amounts of iron tends to have lower
levels of potassium.

- **(a)** Two variables: amount of iron in the soil (**quantitative**) and potassium
  level in the spinach (**quantitative**).
- **(b)** The amount of iron in the soil is the **explanatory** variable; potassium
  level is the response.
- **(c)** **Observational study** — locations were sampled as found; nothing was
  applied or assigned.
- **(d) No.** Observational data cannot establish that iron in the soil *causes*
  lower potassium in the spinach.
- **(e) Possible confounder: the overall soil type/composition (or climate) of the
  location.** Locations with iron-rich soil may differ systematically in other soil
  minerals or conditions that affect how much potassium spinach absorbs — a
  variable associated with soil iron that also directly influences potassium levels.

## Exercise 1.104

**Encourage Kids to Read!** Researchers asked parents of 19 American children
(ages 8–12) about hours spent reading and on screen-based media; each child also
underwent MRI to assess brain connectivity. More reading was associated with higher
connectivity; more screen time with lower connectivity.

- **(a)** **19 cases** (the children) and **3 variables**.
- **(b)** All three variables are **quantitative** (hours of reading, hours of
  screen media, brain connectivity). **Explanatory variables:** reading hours and
  screen-time hours; **response variable:** brain connectivity.
- **(c)** **Observational study** — reading and screen habits were reported, not
  assigned.
- **(d) No.** With no random assignment (and only 19 children), we cannot conclude
  that reading *increases* connectivity; the study shows an association only.
- **(e) Possible confounder: parental involvement (or family income).** Parents who
  strongly encourage reading may also provide other enriching experiences.
  Parental engagement is associated with the child’s reading hours and can
  itself influence brain development, fitting the definition of a confounder.

## Exercise 1.105

**Want to Be Healthier? Take a Vacation!** Health characteristics (triglycerides,
cholesterol, blood glucose) were measured for 63 adults, who also reported how many
vacations they had taken in the last year. More vacations went along with better
health measures.

- **(a)** **Observational study.**
- **(b) Confounder: income (or wealth).** People with higher incomes take more
  vacations and generally have better healthcare, nutrition, and working
  conditions. Income is associated with taking vacations and itself influences
  health — the definition of a confounding variable.
- **(c)** Appropriate conclusions from this study:
  - **(i) Yes** — the observed association is consistent with this (association is
    symmetric: healthier people do take more vacations).
  - **(ii) Yes** — this is the association as reported.
  - **(iii) No** — a causal claim, not warranted from an observational study.
  - **(iv) No** — also a causal claim (in the reverse direction).
- **(d) No.** The title “Take a Vacation!” implies that taking vacations *will*
  improve health — a causal conclusion the study cannot support.

## Exercise 1.106

**Do Online Cat Videos Improve Mood?** People who clicked on a link were asked
about their mood before and after the most recent time they watched a cat video.
Participants reported more energy and more positive emotions afterwards. Can we
conclude that watching cat videos increases energy and improves emotional state?

- **No.** This is an observational study: participants *chose* whether and when to
  watch the videos, and no comparison group was randomly assigned. Self-selected
  participants may differ systematically, and expectation effects are possible, so
  the before/after differences show association — not causation.

## Exercise 1.107

**Green Spaces Make Kids Smarter.** The study involved 2623 schoolchildren in
Barcelona: researchers measured greenery around each school and the children’s
working memories and attention spans. More vegetation went along with better
memory and attention.

- **(a) Cases:** the 2623 schoolchildren.
- **(b) Explanatory variable:** the amount of greenery around the child’s school.
- **(c) Response variable:** working memory and attention span (test performance).
- **(d) Yes** — “make kids smarter” is causal language.
- **(e)** **Observational study** — greenery was measured, not assigned.
- **(f) No** — it is not appropriate to conclude causation from this study.
- **(g) Confounder: neighborhood wealth / school funding.** Wealthier neighborhoods
  have both more greenery and better-resourced schools (and families with more
  resources). Wealth is associated with the explanatory variable and itself
  influences the response, satisfying the definition of a confounding variable.

## Exercise 1.108

**Infections Can Lower IQ.** Scientists gave an IQ test to Danish men at age 19 and
examined their hospital records: 35% had been hospitalized with an infection, and
average IQ was lower for the men who had.

- **(a) Cases:** the Danish men who were tested.
- **(b) Explanatory variable:** whether the man had been hospitalized with an
  infection (yes / no) — **categorical**.
- **(c) Response variable:** IQ score — **quantitative**.
- **(d) Yes** — “can lower IQ” implies causation.
- **(e)** **Observational study** — infections were not assigned; existing records
  were analyzed.
- **(f) No.** Because the men were not randomly assigned, confounding variables
  (e.g., socioeconomic background, which affects both infection risk and IQ
  scores) prevent a causal conclusion.

## Exercise 1.109

**Sitting Is the New Smoking.** A large 2015 study followed 69,260 men and 77,462
women; among women, those who spent more leisure time sitting were significantly
more likely to get cancer.

- **(a) Explanatory variable:** amount of leisure time spent sitting
  (**quantitative**, possibly grouped into levels); **response variable:** whether
  the woman developed cancer (**categorical**).
- **(b)** **Observational study** — a cohort followed over time; no one was assigned
  to a sitting regimen.
- **(c) No.** The study shows an association. Women who sit more may differ in
  exercise habits, weight, diet, or healthcare access, and any of these could
  account for the difference, so causation is not established.
- **(d) No.** The study cannot show that sitting *does not* cause cancer — it found
  an association, and failure to prove causation is not evidence of no causation.

## Exercise 1.110

**Late Night Eating.** 44 people aged 21–50 were limited to 4 hours of sleep per
night for three nights. On the fourth night all stayed up until 4 am, but they
were *randomized* into two groups: one had access only to water from 10 pm, while
the other kept unlimited access to food and drink. The fasting group performed
significantly better on reaction-time tests and had fewer attention lapses.

- **(a) Explanatory variable:** late-night access to food (food and drink vs water
  only) — **categorical**; **response variable:** performance on reaction-time and
  attention tests (**quantitative**).
- **(b)** **Randomized experiment** — participants were randomized to the two
  late-night conditions.
- **(c) Yes.** Because the explanatory variable was randomly assigned, the group
  difference in performance can reasonably be attributed to the late-night eating
  itself: eating late at night worsens some of the typical effects of sleep
  deprivation.
- **(d) No — confounding variables are unlikely to be a problem.** Randomization
  balances confounders (age, sleep habits, diet, ...) between the two groups on
  average, which is exactly why randomized experiments support causal conclusions.

## Exercise 1.111

**Does Early Language Reduce Tantrums?** A study recorded the language skill level
and the number of tantrums for a sample of preschoolers; early language skills
were associated with fewer tantrums.

- **(a)** **Observational study.**
- **(b) No.** “Reduce” is causal language, but the study supports at most an
  association between language skills and tantrums — no treatment was assigned.
- **(c) Potential confounder: age.** Older preschoolers tend to have better
  language skills *and* fewer tantrums, so age is associated with the explanatory
  variable and directly influences the response. (Parenting quality would be
  another reasonable choice.)

## Exercise 1.112

**Does Buying Organic Food Improve Your Health?** In the 2009–2010 NHANES survey,
46% of people who had bought organic food reported their health as very good or
excellent, versus only 33% of those who had not. Three possible explanations:
(i) causal association, (ii) association due to confounding, (iii) no actual
association (chance).

- **(a) No.** NHANES simply records what people already do — nothing is assigned —
  so the study provides no evidence that the two groups were comparable to begin
  with. There is no randomization to balance the groups, so confounding is very
  much alive.
- **(b) Potential confounder: income (or general health consciousness).** People
  who buy organic tend to be wealthier, and income also buys better healthcare and
  healthier food overall; the health-conscious also exercise more and smoke less.
- **(c) No.** Because explanation (ii) — confounding — has not been ruled out, the
  study does not provide convincing evidence that buying organic food improves
  general health.

*Data:* `data/ch01/NHANES.csv` (NHANES 2009–2010 subset, n = 4716), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/NHANES.csv>. The file reproduces the numbers
in the exercise: 46% vs 33% report very good or excellent health — and it also
exposes the confounder:

```{python}
#| echo: false
nh = pd.read_csv("data/ch01/NHANES.csv")
nh.head()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pct = nh.groupby("Organic")["HealthBinary"].apply(
    lambda s: (s == "Very good / Excellent").mean())
pd.DataFrame({
    "n": nh.groupby("Organic").size(),
    "Pct very good/excellent health": (pct * 100).round(1),
    "Mean income": nh.groupby("Organic")["Income"].mean().round(0),
})
```

Organic buyers do report better health — but they also earn about \$1000 more on
average, the very confounding described in (b):

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Self-reported health by organic-food purchase, as proportions within each group
ct = pd.crosstab(nh["Organic"], nh["Health"], normalize="index")[
    ["Poor", "Fair", "Good", "Very good", "Excellent"]]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
ct.plot.bar(ax=ax, rot=0,
            color=["#c44e52", "#dd8452", "#ccb974", "#4c72b0", "#2f5f8f"])
ax.set_xlabel("Bought organic food")
ax.set_ylabel("Proportion")
ax.legend(title="Health", fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Exercise 1.113

**Does Eating Organic Food Make Fruit Flies Live Longer?** For a high-school
science project, a 16-year-old *randomly divided* fruit flies into two groups, fed
one group organic food and the other conventional food, and found the organic group
lived an average of 3.25 days longer.

- **(a) Yes.** The flies were **randomly divided** into the two groups, so
  confounding variables (sex, age, genetics, cage conditions, ...) are balanced
  between groups by design. The study provides evidence against explanation (ii):
  the groups did not differ to begin with.
- **(b)** Not needed here — randomization means there should be no *systematic*
  difference between the groups at the outset. (In a small sample the groups could
  still differ by chance, but that is explanation (iii), not confounding.)
- **(c) Yes.** With random assignment ruling out confounding, and explanation (iii)
  (chance) addressed in Chapter 5, the evidence supports the causal conclusion that
  eating organic food causes fruit flies to live longer — in this experiment, at
  least.

## Exercise 1.114

**Goldilocks Effect: Read to Your Kids! (Part 2).** Each of 27 four-year-olds was
presented with stories in all three formats (audio, illustrated, animated) while an
MRI machine measured brain connectivity. Audio and animation showed low
connectivity; the illustrated format showed the highest.

- **(a)** **A matched pairs type experiment.** Each child is measured under *all
  three* conditions, so each child serves as their own control, and the formats are
  actively presented by the researchers. (More generally, a within-subjects
  randomized experiment.)
- **(b) Yes.** Because the treatments were imposed on the children and each child is
  compared against themselves, we can conclude that the illustrated format produces
  higher brain connectivity than listening to a story or watching an animated
  version for children like these.
- **(c)** Randomization should determine the **order** in which each child
  experiences the three formats (randomly permuted for each child), so that order
  or fatigue effects cannot favor one format over the others.

## Exercise 1.115

**Sleep and Recognition of Facial Expressions.** 18 healthy young adults were shown
70 images of facial expressions both after a full night of sleep and after 24 hours
awake, with the order randomly determined. People were much worse at recognizing
expressions after being kept awake.

- **(a) Explanatory variable:** sleep condition (full night’s sleep vs sleep
  deprived) — **categorical**; **response variable:** ability to recognize facial
  expressions, e.g. accuracy on the 70 images — **quantitative**.
- **(b)** **Randomized experiment** — and since every volunteer is tested under both
  conditions, it is a **matched pairs** experiment.
- **(c) Yes.** The condition (and its order) was randomly assigned, so the worse
  performance after sleep deprivation can be attributed causally to missing a night
  of sleep.
- **(d) No.** Here the explanatory variable — quality of REM sleep — was **not
  randomly assigned**; it is an observed characteristic, so this part is an
  observational comparison. Confounding variables (e.g., overall sleep health)
  prevent a causal conclusion.

## Exercise 1.116

**Diet Cola and Weight Gain in Humans.** American senior citizens who drink diet
soda regularly experience a greater increase in weight and waist circumference than
those who do not.

- **(a) No.** This is an observational study, so confounding is possible: for
  example, people who are already gaining weight may *switch* to diet soda
  (reverse causation), or diet-soda drinkers may differ in overall diet or health
  consciousness. The association alone does not establish that diet soda causes
  weight gain.
- **(b)** Together the two studies strengthen the case: the randomized rat
  experiment (Exercise 1.70) shows that in a controlled setting the association
  persists even without confounding, which makes the causal explanation more
  plausible for humans as well. Still, the human evidence remains observational —
  so the combined studies suggest diet cola *may* cause weight gain in humans, but
  they do not prove it.

## Exercise 1.117

**Urban Brains and Rural Brains.** A 2010 study showed city dwellers have a 21%
higher risk of anxiety disorders and a 39% higher risk of mood disorders. A 2011
follow-up scanned the brains of city and country dwellers during a stressful math
test and found greater activity in stress centers for urban dwellers.

- **(a)** The 2010 study is an **observational study** — people already lived where
  they lived.
- **(b) No.** Confounding variables (income, lifestyle, access to healthcare, ...)
  could explain the difference, so causation cannot be concluded.
- **(c)** The 2011 study is also an **observational study** with respect to living
  location — dwelling was not assigned (only the stressful test was imposed on
  everyone).
- **(d)** Explanatory variable: whether the person lives in a city or the country —
  **categorical**. Response variable: level of activity in the stress centers of
  the brain — **quantitative**.
- **(e) No.** The 2011 study is still observational; people were not randomly
  assigned to live in cities, so confounding variables could account for the
  different brain activity.

## Exercise 1.118

**Split the Bill?** Suppose you design an experiment to see whether agreeing in
advance to split a restaurant bill equally affects what people order. The
variables recorded are the type of payment (split or individual), the sex of each
person, the number of items ordered, and the cost of each person’s order. Identify
which variables are explanatory and which are response, and whether each
explanatory variable should be randomly assigned.

- **Explanatory variables:**
  - **Payment type (split vs individual)** — the treatment whose effect on ordering
    is of interest. It **should be randomly assigned**: for example, randomly
    decide which tables pay individually and which agree to split the bill, so
    that the two kinds of tables are comparable otherwise.
  - **Sex** — a pre-existing characteristic that may also help explain what people
    order, so it is explanatory, but it **cannot (and should not) be randomly
    assigned**.
- **Response variables:** the number of items ordered and the cost of each
  person’s order.

*Data:* `data/ch01/SplitBill.csv` (n = 48), downloaded from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/SplitBill.csv> — data from exactly this

## Exercise 1.119

**Be Sure to Get Your Beauty Sleep!** 23 subjects were photographed twice — once
after a good night’s sleep and once after being kept awake for 31 hours — with
hair, make-up, clothing, and lighting identical. Observers rated the photographs
for attractiveness, and the two averages were compared.

- **(a) Explanatory variable:** sleep condition (well rested vs sleep deprived) —
  **categorical**; **response variable:** attractiveness rating given by the
  observers — **quantitative**.
- **(b)** **Experiment** — the sleep condition was imposed. Because each subject
  appears in both photographs, it is a **matched pairs** design.
- **(c) Yes.** Only the sleep differed between the two photographs of the same
  face; everything else was held constant, and observers (blind to condition)
  rated the sleep-deprived photos lower. Sleep deprivation *causes* people to look
  less attractive, as measured by these ratings.

## Exercise 1.120

**Do Antidepressants Work?** Design a randomized comparative experiment to test
whether fluoxetine is effective at reducing depression, using 50 participants and
the change on a standard depression questionnaire as the response variable.

- **(a) Randomization:** randomly divide the 50 participants into two groups of 25;
  one group receives fluoxetine for the study period, the other does not. Random
  assignment balances severity of depression and all other background variables
  between the groups.
- **(b) Placebo:** the control group receives an identical-looking pill with no
  active ingredient, so expectations (the placebo effect) are comparable in the
  two groups and any difference can be attributed to the fluoxetine itself.
- **(c) Double-blind:** neither the participants nor the people who interact with
  them and record the questionnaire scores know who is taking fluoxetine; only,
  say, the statistician analyzing the data knows the group labels.

## Exercise 1.121

**Do Children Need Sleep to Grow?** About 60% of a child’s growth hormone is
secreted during sleep, so lack of sleep might stunt growth.

- **(a)** Explanatory variable: amount of sleep (e.g., reduced sleep vs normal
  sleep); response variable: growth, such as height gained over the study period
  (or a measured growth-hormone level).
- **(b)** Randomized comparative experiment: recruit children and, with consent,
  randomly assign some to a reduced-sleep schedule and others to their normal
  sleep schedule for a fixed period; then compare the average growth of the two
  groups.
- **(c)** It is difficult and unethical because deliberately depriving children of
  sleep could stunt their growth — a serious and possibly permanent harm inflicted
  with no compensating benefit to the child — and guardians would be unlikely to
  consent. So objective experimental verification is hard to obtain, and we rely
  on observational evidence.

## Exercise 1.122

**Carbo Loading.** Does carbo loading (eating lots of carbohydrates the day
before) actually improve athletic performance the following day? You recruit 50
athletes.

- **(a) Randomized comparative experiment:** randomly split the 50 athletes into
  two groups; one group eats a high-carbohydrate diet the day before the test and
  the other eats a normal (lower-carb) diet. All athletes then complete the same
  endurance test, and the two groups’ performances are compared.
- **(b) Matched pairs experiment:** each athlete completes the endurance test
  twice — once after a day of carbo loading and once after a day of normal eating —
  with the order of the two conditions randomly assigned for each athlete and
  enough recovery time between tests. Each athlete’s two performances are then
  compared.
- **(c)** The **matched pairs** design is better here. Athletic ability varies
  enormously from person to person, and matching each athlete against themselves
  removes that person-to-person variability, making it much easier to detect a
  real effect of the carbohydrate loading.

## Exercise 1.123

**Alcohol and Reaction Time.** Design a randomized experiment on 40 college
seniors, with the response variable the time to react to an image on a screen
after drinking either alcohol or water.

- **(a) A randomized comparative experiment:** randomly divide the 40 seniors into
  two groups of 20 — randomization decides who drinks alcohol and who drinks
  water — then measure each person’s reaction time and compare the average
  reaction times of the two groups.
- **(b) A matched pairs experiment:** every senior takes the reaction-time test
  twice, once after drinking alcohol and once after drinking water, with the order
  of the two conditions randomly assigned for each participant (and enough time
  allowed between for the alcohol to wear off). Each person’s two reaction times
  are compared.

## Exercise 1.124

**Causation and Confounding.** Causation does not necessarily mean that there is
no confounding variable. Give an example of an association between two variables
that have a causal relationship *and* have a confounding variable.

- **Example:** amount of fertilizer used and crop yield. Fertilizer genuinely
  *causes* higher yields, yet the observed association is also partly confounded
  by **soil quality**: farmers with better soil tend to use more fertilizer (they
  expect more from good fields), and good soil itself produces higher yields. Soil
  quality is associated with fertilizer use and also directly affects yield — a
  confounding variable coexisting with a genuine causal relationship.
- (Another valid example: exercise and fitness, confounded by a health-conscious
  diet — people who exercise also tend to eat better, and diet directly affects
  fitness.)

:::
